description: In this team, we believe that all we need is coffee and a sleepless weekend to do anything.
summary:
SATASPY started with a pretty simple idea. We wanted people to learn about space by actually doing things, not just reading about them.
We built 21 interactive mini games and labs based on real science and NASA's publicly available research. Players can experiment with engineering, programming, orbital mechanics and even lunar exploration. The first chapter also supports 5 languages.
But we didn't want to make a bunch of science activities and call it a game. We wanted something people would actually enjoy playing.
That's why we spent so much time on the story. We designed 5 chapters with different characters, personalities and choices that can completely change where your agency ends up. We also worked on keeping the characters, backgrounds and other artwork in the same style.
You might start out wanting to do something great for science, but money, politics and ambition can slowly change your priorities. Your decisions affect the story, the people around you and which of the 4 planned endings you reach.
We wanted to make a game people could genuinely get invested in, while learning real science along the way.
details:
SATASPY is a browser game where you get to run your own space agency. You start by choosing your country from an interactive 3D Earth with 197 countries available, then you get your own agency, a small budget and a team of people you'll be working with throughout the game.

When we first started working on SATASPY, we knew we didn't want to make another educational game where you just answer questions and move on. We wanted people to actually enjoy playing it, even if they weren't particularly interested in space or science.

That's why we spent so much time on the story. We planned it across 5 chapters, starting with something relatively simple like launching your first satellite, but eventually getting into much bigger things like international competition, commercial contracts, strange discoveries, sending people into space and trying to establish a research station on the Moon.

And the story can go in very different directions depending on what you do. We didn't want players to feel like their choices were just there for decoration. Decisions you make early on can affect things much later, including your relationships with the characters, the missions you can take on and whether your agency even survives.

One thing we really wanted to explore was how easily an organization can lose track of why it was created in the first place. You might start out wanting to do something good for science, but then you need money to keep going, the government wants results, companies offer you contracts and suddenly you're making compromises you never planned on making. We designed 4 different endings around that idea. You might actually achieve your dream of reaching the Moon, end up running something completely different or lose everything you've worked for.

We also wanted the characters to feel like actual people. They have different personalities, opinions and problems of their own, and they won't always agree with you. We put a lot of work into their designs and the backgrounds too, making sure everything followed the same visual style so the whole game felt like it belonged together.

Of course, the science is still a huge part of SATASPY. We made 21 interactive mini games and labs that cover different subjects including programming, engineering, communications, orbital mechanics, robotics, lunar geology and life support.

We tried to make each lab something you can actually experiment with. In one of them you work with a 3D Earth to plan satellite orbits and understand communication windows. In another you program a rover, and in others you test spacecraft materials, analyze satellite observations or deal with the challenges of keeping astronauts alive in space.

We didn't just invent the science behind these activities either. We went through publicly available NASA research and educational materials and used real resources like Blue Marble imagery, ISS orbital data, MODIS observations and lunar maps. We did simplify some calculations because it's still a game and we want people to understand what's happening, but we tried to keep the actual scientific principles as accurate as possible.

There's also Mission Studio, which is a separate part of the game where you can design an entire space mission yourself. You choose what you want the mission to achieve, what spacecraft and instruments to use, how to launch it and which orbit works best. You also have to think about things like power, mass, budget and communications. Once you're done, you can simulate the mission and see what went right or wrong.

On the technical side, we built the game using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Three.js, Zustand and Vite. It's playable on computers and phones. We also added support for English, Turkish, Spanish, Japanese and Arabic in the first chapter, although some translations still need reviewing and the later chapters are currently in English.

Another thing we thought was important was letting people access the mini games without having to finish the story first. So we made them available separately from the main menu. Someone who just wants to try the orbital simulator or learn about rocket propulsion can do that without spending hours playing through the campaign.

What we really hope to achieve with SATASPY is getting people interested in things they might never have thought about learning before. Not everyone is going to open a textbook about orbital mechanics for fun, and that's completely understandable. But if you're playing a game, you care about your characters and your next mission depends on understanding how an orbit works, you might actually want to learn it.

And that's basically the whole idea behind SATASPY. We wanted to make a game with a story people can get invested in, characters they'll remember and choices that genuinely matter, while making real science part of the experience instead of something that feels like homework.
